name: AHK-Cu
lead: AHK-Cu is a copper complex of the tripeptide alanyl-histidyl-lysine, also called copper tripeptide-3. It is marketed in hair-care products and discussed in appearance circles as a hair-growth ingredient, in the way the related GHK-Cu is discussed for skin [1].
Published evidence is limited to a laboratory study on cultured human hair follicle cells. No human trial of AHK-Cu for hair growth was found.

paras: AHK-Cu is related to GHK-Cu, a copper complex of glycyl-histidyl-lysine first isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in the 1970s and used in cosmetics under the name copper tripeptide-1. The Wikipedia article on GHK-Cu mentions AHK-Cu only as a related topic and gives no description of it.

A 2007 in vitro study reported that a tripeptide-copper complex stimulated proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and raised production of vascular endothelial growth factor while reducing secretion of transforming growth factor-beta1, and examined effects on human dermal papilla cells and hair growth in culture [1].

No studies found. A registered early phase 1 trial of systemic and topical interventions assessed with aging clocks (NCT07888595) was listed as enrolling by invitation; its relevance to hair outcomes is not established [2].

card.summary: A copper tripeptide marketed for hair growth, backed so far only by cell-culture research.

quick.overview:
AHK-Cu is a copper-bound three-amino-acid peptide sold in hair products and related to the better-known GHK-Cu.

The main published work is a lab study on cultured follicle cells. Human results are not available.
quick.mechanism: In cell culture, a tripeptide-copper complex was reported to boost fibroblast growth and VEGF, and to act on dermal papilla cells, the cells that steer hair follicle growth.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy data specific to AHK-Cu were found.
